newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Swaps traders see two-faced sword in EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swaps traders see two-faced sword in EMU.

text.p: Uncertainties about EMU should make dealers in the swaps market, which thrives on interest rate uncertainty, busier and better paid than ever.
But if a half-dozen or so of the world's currencies become one, these traders will also be faced with the possibility that volumes in the multi-trillion dollar market will be eroded.

"EMU may be a golden opportunity due to increased volatility, but in the long term (when EMU works smoothly), it may be a real depressant of swap volumes," said David Gelber, managing director at derivatives broker Intercapital.

The technical path to EMU has been going smoothly, dealers said, as most of the legal issues are being resolved and other outstanding problems -- such as what will happen to Ecu contracts -- do not affect the majority of contracts.

But in terms of trading during the transition to European economic and monetary union (EMU), the swaps market is wary amid uncertainty over how stringently the qualifying criteria will be interpreted and thus, which countries will join by 1999.
There could be tremendous volatility and yield changes, both among currencies that will be in and those that will be out of the euro, dealers said.
"(This) could lead to a lot more hedging, but it is not happening yet," said a senior derivatives trader at SBC Warburg.
"People do not yet have a good enough feel for what will actually happen," he said.

What is certain though is the volume of currency swaps -- deals in which different currencies are exchanged with an agreement to re-exchange at the same exchange rate when the swap terminates -- will fall when EMU is fully in place, dealers said.

But currency swaps only total $1.2 trillion, compared with the more than $12 trillion of interest rate swaps outstanding, according to International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) figures for 1995.
"Players are obviously very worried about the amount of business we will have after EMU," said the SBC Warburg trader.
"But I think the euro will be of similar size to the dollar market, and volumes in dollar interest rate swaps alone are far greater than trades involving European currencies," he said.
"There is no reason why euro interest rate swaps should not also be big business," he said.
"There is a strong liklihood the euro will become another reserve currency like the dollar and yen," said Clifford Dammers, secretary general of IPMA, the International Primary Market Association.
Dollar interest rate swaps accounted for 34 percent, or $4.4 trillion, of total outstanding deals at the end of 1995. Yen transactions totalled $2.9 trillion, or 22.6 percent.
The aggregate of swaps in marks, French francs, Belgian francs and guilder amounted to $2.3 trillion equivalent.

Interest rate swaps are an exchange of interest payments, from a fixed to floating rate or vice-versa. They allow firms to manage interest rate exposure by, for instance, locking in fixed rates while interest rates are low.

Interest rate swaps are also widely used to minimise funding costs by borrowing in markets where an entity has a comparative advantage and to gain the desired interest rate exposure. Such "plain vanilla" swaps provide the bulk of business.
Market particpants are upbeat about the chances of maintaining the legality of existing swap contracts denominated in currencies that could soon be extinct.
"The plain-vanilla cases, which are 90 percent of cases, are not a problem," said IPMA's Dammers.

"The good news is the most recent version of the legal draft (released in September) providing for the introduction of the euro is in pretty good shape because the European Commission has listened to the market," said Dammers.
"(Legally) it is only a problem when the contract gets complicated by, for example, if pricing sources disappear or the transaction changes from a hedge to an annuity."
Industry bodies have geared up their efforts to influence the debate and tackle the minutiae of swap contracts.
"Much of our work related to EMU derives from our desire to ensure the legal certainty of privately negotiated derivatives contracts," said Gay Evans, chairman of ISDA.

To get a better understanding of the implications for swaps in EMU, the ISDA has set up taskforces to look at the impacts on legislative and regulatory issues, documentation, market practices and tax, accounting and capital issues of EMU.
There are technical issues that need to be resolved.

"One example is...interest rate calculation convention and rate sources. Harmonisation of interest rate calculation would be helpful, and maintenance of quote sources until all relevant contracts had expired would aid in preventing windfall gains or losses," she said.
One peripheral area that remains a problem is the status of Ecu-denominated contracts.
"There are big concerns about existing contracts, especially Ecu-denominated ones," said a swaps trader at a U.S. bank.
"There is a question whether the Ecu will exist as a separate currency or whether it will be replaced by the euro. This will likely be resolved in court."
ISDA figures show just $223 million in Ecu interest-rate swaps outstanding at the end of last year and $50 million in Ecu currency swaps.
London-based dealers said whether or not sterling took part in EMU was unlikely to affect their job prospects.
"London will remain the centre of (European swap) business regardless," said the U.S. bank's swap trader.
"Even if the French or Germans try to devise regulations to bring business there, the market will always find a way around them. Anyone should be able to have access to the euro."
